newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says no to NATO summit, works on holiday.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says no to NATO summit, works on holiday.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has no plans to attend next July's NATO summit which is due to offer membership to some former Soviet bloc states, Interfax news agency quoted his spokesman as saying on Saturday.

"I will venture to say that participation at the forthcoming Madrid meeting...has never been seriously considered by the top Russian leadership," said Sergei Yastrzhembsky, noting that the Madrid summit did not appear on Yeltsin's working schedule.
Kremlin officials contacted directly declined to comment or say whether the decision reflected any change in Yeltsin's determination to sign a treaty with NATO a month from now.

Yastrzhembsky, who was speaking to Interfax in the Black Sea resort of Sochi where Yeltsin is on holiday, said the Russian position on attending did not depend on getting an invitation to Madrid from the Western defence pact.
He added that Russian officials had plenty of opportunity to exchange opinions with NATO and its leading members.
Russian officials led by Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov are urgently negotiating a treaty on Russian-NATO relations which Yeltsin said last week he would sign in Paris on May 27.
The Kremlin, vehemently opposed to NATO expansion, wants a say in the enlarged bloc and formal guarantees on its security.
Some Western negotiators, notably in Washington, doubt that differences between the two sides can be overcome in a month.
Some Western officials had appeared to believe Yeltsin would attend the Madrid meeting if a deal was reached, but the Kremlin had previously said it was not sure that the president would go.

The issue of membership invitations to countries such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- which some will read as a symbol of Western victory in the Cold War -- will remain a sore moment for Russia even if it signs a treaty with NATO.
Yeltsin worked and strolled in the grounds of his vacation retreat on Saturday despite cool weather and drizzle, Yastrzhembsky told Interfax.
"The president has just gone out for a walk in the park," he said shortly after midday, noting there was a fine drizzle and the temperature was just 12 degrees Celsius (54 Fahrenheit).
The spokesman said Yeltsin, 66, "worked fully on papers" to produce a number of decrees and decisions, some of which were published by the Kremlin press service.

Yeltsin sent a letter to the communist speaker of the State Duma, Gennady Seleznyov, telling parliament to work with the government on drawing up urgent amendments to the labour code in order to correct flaws and ensure companies provided proper working conditions for their employees.

The press service said he also appointed the 30-year-old Anton Danilov-Danilyan, an economist and the son of Russia's top environmental official, to head the economics department of the presidential administration.
In a strongly-worded radio address on Thursday, Yeltsin criticised Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and regional leaders for failing to appoint more young administrators.

Yastrzhembsky told Interfax that Yeltsin's remarks should be viewed as "an address to the whole leadership" but should not be taken as a prelude to a new government shake-up. Yeltsin appointed a youthful new team, led by first deputy premiers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, only last month.
